column3: Retrospective regret links failed hearing and reasoning to belonging among the Fire's people, but not to misclassifying absent men.
Building for imagined permanence does not develop sight, social counting, or the missing men.
A false, self-protective assessment of the Fire parallels the speakers' earlier bad classification, though the objects differ.
Elites dismiss followers as socially low and call them liars, closely paralleling contemptuous human classification.
The surrounding section's praise of servants endowed with insight reverses the scene's failure to recognize worthy men.
The promised reality becomes visible and overturns its deniers' prior stance, a broader pattern of corrective sight.
Showing the promised punishment would correct the addressee's horizon, but does not involve social misclassification.
The immediate continuation explicitly asks whether mockery or deviated sight explains the missing men.
Seeing a destroyed people supports sight as evidential inspection, without the focus's classification or absence.
Demanding a visible sign is a different misuse of sight from overlooking those already judged contemptibly.
Mocking believers turns them into objects of derision, directly paralleling the earlier treatment of the missing men.
Calling disbelievers the worst creatures offers a moral classification, but not the focus's exposed human miscount.
Denial of resurrection lacks the focus's sight and social-ranking relation.
The same local sequence grounds the honored servants in remembrance of the final abode, against the speakers' defective final assessment.
Inability to count divine blessings does not clarify counting people as evil.
The absence of intercessors in the Fire gives a limited parallel to the speakers' discovery that expected people are missing.
The local catalogue of hostile factions provides only broad opposition context for the later Fire scene.
Uncertainty whether an outcome is evil or rightly guided cautions against the focus's confident evil classification.
Seeing part of a promised outcome concerns prophetic reassurance, not the social field of view in the focus.
Covering imagery has only an indirect relation to the possibility of sight departing from its object.
Divine counting of people contrasts only distantly with the speakers' earlier social count.
Final exposure dissolves former hierarchy and dependence, providing a broader correction to worldly social judgments.
The local declaration that the servants are the chosen excellent ones directly reverses counting persons among the evil.
It distinguishes truthful perception from falsehood, supporting the question whether the speakers' sight has gone astray.
Confession of prior error is a general retrospective correction, without the focus's visual or classificatory structure.
This earlier narrative action does not clarify the absent men or distorted sight.
God's exhaustive individual count contrasts with the speakers' coarse and false grouping of men as evil.
A promised outcome may be shown, but the verse does not address the focus's missing social group.
Prior false assumptions about speech about God offer only a general warning against ungrounded judgments.
Its final moral ranking of disbelievers supplies a genuine but differently grounded category of evil.
Demanding to see God displays a distorted condition for recognition, a broader counterpart to failed sight in the focus.
The local designation of further servants as excellent continues the reversal of the focus's bad classification.
Unseen forces show that the visible field is incomplete, but do not explain the missing men.
Recognizing men by their marks and reproving their arrogance closely parallels social identification within the hereafter.
The preceding exchange in the Fire establishes the speakers' hostile scene but not the missing-men question itself.
Counting a few coins concerns valuation in trade, not counting persons among the evil.
Seeing promised punishment offers only the general pattern of later corrective disclosure.
Visible lightning is unrelated to moral classification or the absence of persons from sight.
Seeing one's evil deed is individual final accountability, not the focus's mistaken assessment of others.
Impatiently demanding one's record before judgment provides only broad final-account context.
Solomon's request for dominion has no focused route to distorted social sight.
Human counting of time concerns impatience over punishment, not counting men as evil.
Messengers are human men receiving revelation, countering a contemptuous treatment of men as merely evil.
Its human and jinn men are social categories, but the protection relation does not develop the focus's judgment.
Seeing renewed earth infers hidden agency, only broadly related to sight's limits.
Like 16:43, it identifies divinely sent human men and supplies a corrective category for judging men.
The immediate complaint about those who led them into punishment frames the hostile attribution just before the focus.
The absence of harsh climate from Paradise is literal perception without a social-recognition link.
Men arriving for pilgrimage are unrelated to the focus's missing group and moral ranking.
The location of the lote tree does not add to the focus's distorted sight question.
What people dislike may be good and what they like evil, directly cautioning against surface moral classification.
Turning away from idle speech does not address sight, counting, or absent persons.
The earlier list of deniers gives broad local opposition context only.
Divine hearing and seeing reassure Musa and Harun, without the focus's mistaken perception of others.
Final gratitude for guidance contrasts broadly with prior error, but has no direct missing-men relation.
The contrast between blind and seeing gives a compact analogue for the focus's possible visual deviation.
Seeing great signs affirms reliable perception, contrasting with sight that may have strayed from its objects.
Human men as revealed-to messengers and the call to inspect prior outcomes both challenge contemptuous social reading.
The local dispute scene has no direct route to the Fire's missing-men question.
Manipulating counted months is a different kind of false accounting, with little link to social classification.
At final judgment claimed partners are absent from sight, a close formal parallel to discovering expected figures missing.
Nearness imagery does not clarify the focus's social field of view.
A second confirmed sighting supports the distinction between valid perception and perception that has gone astray.
Showing Abraham the dominion builds certainty but does not concern failed recognition of people.
The David narrative remains only distant local context for the later Fire scene.
When the promise is seen, claims about who is worse and weaker in number are corrected, closely matching the focus's failed ranking.
A baseless claim about limited Fire punishment parallels the focus's erroneous confidence within the Fire.
The explicit statement that sight neither deviated nor transgressed directly illuminates the focus's alternative that sight deviated.
Seeing how a former people was treated turns historical consequence into corrective recognition.
Seeing the promised punishment corrects rival claims about who is worse in position and weaker in force.
The description of the mighty figure's poise does not add to the missing-men scene.
Asking those who count about duration concerns temporal reckoning, not social misclassification.
Divine awareness of the messenger's gaze concerns direction, not the focus's failure to see people.
The blind-and-seeing contrast is broad theological imagery, only secondarily related to deviated sight.
Counting accumulated wealth differs from counting men into a moral class.
Human haste in praying for evil offers only a general error-of-judgment parallel.
Refusing belief until punishment is seen reflects a recognition delayed until visible reality overturns prior refusal.
Generic refuge from created evil does not clarify who is rightly classified as evil.
The demand to see God openly shows that sight can be wrongly made a condition of belief.
Envy as a source of evil does not address visual absence or social counting.
An apparent evil is reclassified through its outcome, strongly cautioning against immediate social judgment.
The claim that eyes have been dazzled or bewitched closely parallels the possibility that sight has departed from the missing men.
When punishment is seen, former followers and leaders separate, correcting prior social attachments and judgments.
Believers' question about faith in received truth does not develop the focus's visual misclassification.
Even many signs fail to persuade until punishment is seen, a general pattern of belated corrective sight.
Trust and prayer amid oppression do not clarify the absent men or their classification.
Impressive appearance and speech can mislead perception about people, a strong social-perception parallel.
Claiming to hear while not hearing is a general failure of reception, not the focus's sight question.
Disputing a witness over what he sees contrasts with the focus's uncertainty about its own sight.
Wealth and children are used to claim immunity, another false social self-assessment overturned by judgment.
Misplaced fear reveals lack of understanding, but not misrecognition of the absent men.
Seeing death's punishment is a broad final-disclosure parallel without social classification.
Denying revelation to any human is corrected by Musa's book, countering dismissive judgments about human recipients.
Arrogance makes people reject every sign they see and choose error over guidance, explaining a morally distorted perception.
Visible revival of dead earth supports resurrection, not the missing men's social status.
Seeing people enter God's religion does not address the focus's contemptuous classification.
Humanly imposed names follow conjecture and desire rather than guidance, a close analogue to falsely labeling men evil.
Recognizing the denier through conduct is only a broad pattern of moral discernment.
The command to consume good provision and give thanks has no focused relation.
The parable invites people to see and reflect on a reality weighty enough to correct superficial judgment.
Calling believers fools is a direct worldly counterpart to falsely classifying people by contempt.
Disbelievers mock believers because worldly appearance has been made attractive to them; the final reversal directly fits the focus.
It forbids denying another person's faith from an outward social judgment, directly restraining false classification.
The command not to drive away devoted believers directly opposes contemptuous exclusion of persons from religious standing.
The question whether these are those favored by God exposes an elite's false judgment of socially lesser believers.
Men on the Heights recognize all parties by their marks, providing a hereafter model of accurate human recognition.
Those once thought undeserving of mercy are explicitly admitted to Paradise, closely reversing the focus's earlier contempt.
The Fire's people appeal to Paradise's people after the final separation, extending the scene of belated recognition across the boundary.
Noah rejects the claim that people despised by others will receive no good from God, a direct anticipation of the focus's error.
The messenger must remain with humble worshippers and not let social prestige turn his eyes away from them.
Eyes covered from remembrance show a spiritual failure of sight that can explain missing what ought to be recognized.
Turning from remembrance leads to being raised blind, sharply connecting moral refusal with final perceptual loss.
The raised person's question about being blind despite having seen makes final blindness a reversal of earlier sight.
Forgetting the signs is answered by being forgotten, explaining how prior disregard yields final exclusion.
The verse locates blindness in hearts rather than eyes, directly clarifying how persons can look yet fail to recognize truth.
Those previously mocked are declared the successful ones, completing the reversal already introduced in 23:110.
Making some people a trial for others supplies the social-testing frame behind contemptuous judgments of fellow humans.
Barriers before and behind, with covered sight, provide an image of being unable to see what is present.
The inhabitants of the Fire dispute responsibility among themselves, supplying the same final setting of failed prior judgments.
Unequal worldly provision and rank are assigned as a test, undermining the use of status as a final moral measure.
Disbelievers dismiss believers because they have preceded them to faith, a close parallel to judging people as inferior or evil.
Unrecognized believing men and women are present within a hostile setting, showing that righteous people may be unseen or misjudged.
It expressly forbids ridicule because the mocked may be better than their mockers, the ethical reversal at the core of the focus.
Removal of the veil makes sight sharp, directly countering the focus's possibility of sight having strayed.
Dazzled sight offers a compact eschatological parallel to perceptual failure at judgment.
Criminals laughing at believers is the worldly mockery whose reversal the focus presupposes.
Passing believers with mocking gestures develops the same contemptuous social treatment.
The mockers return to their own people amused, showing their classification is socially reinforced rather than evidential.
Calling believers misguided directly parallels assigning a degrading moral category to them.
Believers laugh at disbelievers on the Day of Judgment, explicitly reversing the earlier mockery.
The final question whether disbelievers have been repaid confirms that the worldly judgment has been overturned.
